Divorce Procedure and Statutory Grounds in Nepal: A Complete Guide

📅 Published: 2025-03-15
🔄 Updated: 2025-10-01
⏱ 9 min read
🔍 Review: Senior Advocate Lead Counsel, Supreme Court Bar Association
Direct Legal Answer & Overview

Under Part 3, Chapter 3 of the Muluki Civil Code 2074 (मुलुकी देवानी संहिता, २०७४), divorce (Sambandh Bichhed / सम्बन्ध विच्छेद) must be formally filed and adjudicated before the competent District Court. A divorce can occur either through Mutual Consent (concluding in 2 to 5 days) or through a Contested Lawsuit on statutory grounds (cruelty, abandonment for 3+ years, adultery). For contested petitions, the court must mandate a conciliation cooling period of up to one year to attempt reconciliation before trial.

Key Practical Takeaways

  • All divorces in Nepal must be decreed by a District Court; municipal ward offices cannot grant legal divorces.
  • Sections 94 (grounds for husband) and 95 (grounds for wife) define explicit statutory grounds.
  • Mutual consent divorce is expedited; contested divorce requires a mandatory 1-year reconciliation attempt.

Divorce law in Nepal underwent a profound modernization with the enactment of the Muluki Civil Code 2074. Previously, legal procedures varied widely, and husbands were forced to navigate complicated municipal ward reconciliation channels. Today, all divorce proceedings are unified under the exclusive jurisdiction of the District Court (जिल्ला अदालत).

1. Statutory Grounds for Divorce under Sections 94 & 95

The Civil Code explicitly defines the legal grounds upon which each spouse may initiate divorce:

Grounds Available to the Husband (Section 94):

  • The wife has been living separately for three or more consecutive years without the husband consent;
  • The wife expels the husband from home or deprives him of maintenance;
  • The wife commits an act causing physical or severe mental cruelty; or
  • The wife engages in sexual intercourse with another person (adultery).

Grounds Available to the Wife (Section 95):

  • The husband has been living separately for three or more consecutive years without consent;
  • The husband expels the wife from home or deprives her of maintenance;
  • The husband commits physical or severe mental cruelty;
  • The husband contracts another marriage (polygamy);
  • The husband engages in sexual intercourse with another person; or
  • The husband rapes the wife (marital rape).

2. Two Paths: Mutual Consent vs. Contested Divorce

If both spouses mutually agree to dissolve the marriage under Section 93, they execute a comprehensive settlement deed covering property division, child custody, and maintenance. Both appear before the District Judge, confirm their consent, and the court issues the final Divorce Decree within 2 to 5 working days.

If the petition is contested, Section 97 mandates that the court must attempt conciliation. The court provides a cooling-off period of up to one year. If reconciliation fails after one year, the court proceeds to full judicial adjudication and renders a final decree.

Statutory Citations & Governing Nepal Legislation

Statute / Act Section / Rule Legal Significance
Muluki Civil Code 2074 Section 93 to 104 (Provisions Relating to Divorce) Core statutory framework for dissolution of marriage, grounds, alimony, and partition.
Muluki Civil Code 2074 Section 97 (Court Conciliation Mandate) Obligation of District Court to conduct reconciliation for up to one year in contested suits.

Documentary Checklist for this Procedure

  • ✔ Official Marriage Registration Certificate (Bibaha Darta)
  • ✔ Nepali Citizenship Certificates of husband and wife (or Passport)
  • ✔ Birth Certificates of minor children (if applicable)
  • ✔ Inventory of marital property for partition (Anshabanda)

Frequently Asked Questions on this Topic

Can a couple get divorced at a municipal ward office in Nepal?

No. Under current Nepalese law, only a District Court has legal jurisdiction to dissolve a marriage. Any divorce document executed merely at a local ward office or on plain paper without a District Court decree is legally void.
